name: Treaty with the Chippewa, etc., 1859 (Swan Creek and Black River Chippewa and Munsee)
aka: Treaty of the Sac and Fox Agency, July 16, 1859
nations: Swan Creek and Black River Chippewa in Kansas
Munsee or Christian Indians in Kansas
promises: Article 1: the 8,320-acre (thirteen-section) reservation in Franklin County, Kansas to benefit the part of the Swan Creek and Black River band living on it, united with the Munsee or Christian Indians as a permanent home.
Article 1: assignments in severalty of up to 40 acres to each head of family and each family member and 80 acres to each unmarried adult, with land kept for a school and held in common.
Article 2: the residue of the band's old tract outside the reduced reservation appraised and sold at auction for no less than its appraised value, the proceeds belonging to the band.
Article 2: $3,000 from the Christian Indians' funds and $6,000 from the Treasury to the Chippewa band, the $6,000 in full satisfaction of all claims under former treaties.
compensation: The sums in Article 2. No Indian Claims Commission decision on this treaty or these Kansas lands was found in the full-text collection under "Swan Creek", "Christian Indians" or "Chippewa Munsee Kansas".
today: The Kansas Chippewa and Munsee were later dissolved as a separate band; treaties.json links them to the Saginaw Chippewa Indian Tribe of Michigan and the Stockbridge Munsee Community. Not researched further.

openQuestions: The later fate of the Franklin County reservation (sale of the land and dissolution of the Chippewa and Munsee band around 1900) and whether the band consented were not researched; that is the most likely place for a breach.
Whether the residue lands in Article 2 were sold at no less than appraised value was not researched.
No account by the Saginaw Chippewa Indian Tribe or the Stockbridge Munsee Community of this treaty was found.

plain.promised: The Swan Creek and Black River Chippewa and the Munsee in Kansas were united on an 8,320-acre reservation in Franklin County, to be divided into family farms, with surplus land sold for their benefit.
plain.happened: No breach has been documented yet in the sources opened.
plain.today: Not settled. What later happened to the Franklin County reservation was not researched.
